title: One virus, many answers: Toward unlocking passion fruit's genetic secrets
content: Engineering plants to meet human demands relies on genomic insights. Despite advances in sequencing, progress in understanding gene functions is slowed by challenges in plant transformation, which is often genotype dependent (Yang B. 2020; Marks et al. 2021). Viruses, although seemingly scary, are versatile vehicles for gene delivery to plants. Viruses are capable of infecting and spreading systemically within plant cells. As a result, plant viruses with RNA or DNA genomes have been widely repurposed as vectors to deliver reagents for numerous genetic engineering applications. However, viruses often can only host a small payload, and larger cargo can make the virus genome unstable (Bruun-Rasmussen 2007). Among the many plant viruses engineered for functional studies, Tobacco rattle virus, which possesses a bipartite ssRNA(+) genome, stands out as the gold standard for virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) and overexpression (VOX) vectors. Its broad host range and versatility have also recently enabled tissue culture–free genome editing (Weiss et al. 2025).
